n: This is one of the most important chapters in the Old Testament. David is settled in his palace, and for a time the Lord has given him peace from his enemies.

f.w: rest round about from all his enemies

n: David tells the prophet Nathan he feels uneasy living in a cedar palace while the ark of God sits in a tent. He wants to build God a temple.

f.g: In a tent, like the tabernacle of Moses’ day.

n: Nathan, sensing David’s good heart, encourages him at once. But he answers before asking the Lord — even a prophet speaks from his own judgment at times.

f.w: Go, do all that is in thine heart

n: That very night the Lord speaks to Nathan with a different message.

f.w: the word of the LORD came unto Nathan

n: The Lord asks David a question that sets up a beautiful wordplay: “Will you build Me a house?” The answer will be that God will build David a house instead.

f.g: “House” means three things in this chapter: a palace, a temple, and a dynasty (royal family line).

n: God reminds David that He has always traveled with His people, living in a tent since the Exodus. He has never needed a permanent building.

f.w: walked in a tent and in a tabernacle

n: In all that time, God never asked any of Israel’s leaders for a cedar temple. The initiative for blessing comes from God, not from human gifts to Him.

f.g: 1 Chronicles 17:6 reads “judges,” which fits the context of leaders who shepherded Israel.

n: God recalls David’s humble beginning: He took him from tending sheep to rule over His people.

f.w: I took thee from the sheepcote

n: The Lord has been with David everywhere, removed his enemies, and made his name great — an echo of God’s promise to Abraham.
God promises a secure homeland where Israel will be planted and no longer harassed by wicked enemies, as they had been in the days of the judges.
Then comes the great reversal: David wanted to build God a house, but the Lord will build David a “house” — a lasting royal dynasty.

f.w: he will make thee an house

n: After David dies, God will raise up one of his own sons and establish his kingdom.

f.g: A gentle idiom for dying and being buried with one’s ancestors.

n: That son — Solomon — will build the temple. And God will establish his throne “for ever,” a promise ultimately fulfilled in Jesus Christ, the Son of David.

f.w: He shall build an house for my name

n: God will relate to David’s son as a father to a son, disciplining him when he sins. Hebrews applies “I will be his father” to Christ, the perfect Son who never needed correction.

f.w: I will be his father, and he shall be my son

f.g: Ordinary human discipline — punishment through people and events.

n: Unlike Saul, David’s line will not lose God’s covenant mercy, even when individual kings fail.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — God’s loyal, covenant love.

f.w: as I took it from Saul

n: David’s house, kingdom, and throne will be established forever. Later prophets looked to this promise in hoping for the Messiah; Latter-day Saints see its fulfillment in Christ, the eternal King.

f.w: thy throne shall be established for ever

n: Nathan faithfully delivers everything the Lord revealed, even though it corrects his own earlier advice.

f.g: A revelation received by a prophet; here a revelation in the night.

n: Overwhelmed, David goes in and sits before the Lord — probably in the tent where the ark was kept — and begins a prayer of humble wonder: “Who am I?”

f.w: Who am I, O Lord GOD?

f.g: When “GOD” is in capitals after “Lord,” the Hebrew is Adonai YHWH — “Lord Jehovah.” Latter-day Saints understand Jehovah as the premortal Jesus Christ.

n: Already God had done much, but now He has promised blessings for David’s descendants far into the future. David marvels at this kind of generous treatment.

f.w: is this the manner of man
f.g: A difficult phrase; possibly “Is this how you deal with mere men?” or “This is instruction for mankind.”

n: David is at a loss for words — God already knows him completely.

f.w: thou, Lord GOD, knowest thy servant

n: God did all this because of His own word and His own heart — out of grace, not because David earned it.
David praises God’s greatness: there is no one like Him, and no other God.
David also praises Israel’s unique story: God personally redeemed them from Egypt to be His own people.
God has made Israel His covenant people forever, and He has become their God.

f.w: a people unto thee for ever

n: David asks God to do exactly what He has promised. Good prayer often takes God’s own words and asks Him to fulfill them.
David’s deepest wish is that God’s name be honored forever, and that his own family remain faithful before Him.
Because God revealed this promise, David found the courage to pray this way. Revelation gives confidence in prayer.
David affirms that God is the true God and that His words can be trusted completely.
He closes by asking God to bless his house forever. This covenant with David becomes a foundation of Israel’s hope for a coming Messiah from David’s line.

f.w: with thy blessing let the house of thy servant be blessed for ever
